First week. Zubin had moved from a quiet Parsi colony in Mumbai to a Delhi school, and at lunch his new classmates talked in a fast, mixed stream: "Bro, scene kya hai?" "Full bakwaas test tha." Zubin answered in careful English and felt like a teacher at the wrong table.
Second week. He tried it. "Scene is... chill?" Suraj laughed, not unkindly. "Almost, yaar. Say 'scene sorted hai'." Zubin practised it on the bus home under his breath.
Fifth week. After the basketball trials, Suraj asked how he felt about being picked as reserve. Zubin opened his mouth for the English word and couldn't find one that fit. "Not sad, exactly. Bas... thoda khalipan." Suraj nodded slowly. "Haan. That's exactly it."
That evening, on the group chat, someone typed "Zubin bhai full desi ho gaya" and Zubin grinned at his phone.

qa.q: What did Suraj teach Zubin to say?
qa.a: Suraj taught him to say "scene sorted hai".

qa.q: How did Zubin feel in the first week at lunch?
qa.a: Zubin felt out of place and awkward, answering in careful English like a teacher at the wrong table while everyone else spoke fast mixed talk.

qa.q: What helped Zubin find his way into the group's talk?
qa.a: Practising small phrases with a friendly guide like Suraj, and using mixed words when English alone could not name what he felt.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Zubin's new way of talking?
qa.a: Suraj is warm and encouraging, correcting gently and nodding when "khalipan" names exactly the feeling Zubin meant.

grounding: A teenager learns to mix Hindi and English to belong, and finds the mix names a feeling one language alone lacks.

"Kiran, you think you invented this 'bro, I'm so done yaar' way of talking? Let your Chandrika Dadi tell you.
"When I was fifteen, in Lucknow, our college crowd thought Hindi alone was for aunties and English alone was for teachers. So we mixed. 'Too much ho gaya.' 'Timepass kar rahe hain.' 'Don't be such a lallu.' My mother would shake her head at the dinner table.
"But one day my best friend Nargis lost her father. At the condolence, I wanted to tell her how I felt and English gave me 'sorry', and Hindi gave me 'dukh'. Neither was enough. I held her hand and said, 'Nargis, I'm here. Tu akeli nahi hai.'
"She told me years later that line stayed with her. Half one language, half the other. That was just how we spoke when we meant it most.

qa.q: Which city did Chandrika Dadi live in at fifteen?
qa.a: She lived in Lucknow.

qa.q: What was young Chandrika feeling when she couldn't find the right word for Nargis?
qa.a: Young Chandrika felt helpless and full of sorrow for her friend, finding that neither "sorry" nor "dukh" was enough.

qa.q: What choice at the condolence mattered, and why?
qa.a: Young Chandrika held Nargis's hand and spoke in mixed Hindi and English, which let her say what one language alone could not.

qa.q: How did Nargis experience Chandrika's words?
qa.a: Nargis felt comforted and less alone, and the mixed line stayed with her for years.

grounding: An elder recalls mixing English and Hindi as a teen to belong, and how the mix expressed what one language lacked.

Rain had stopped the under-sixteen match at the Nashik ground, and the team crowded under the pavilion's tin roof, dripping and bored. Darshan, the newest player, kept to the edge.
The captain, Yash, was holding court. "Bro, this rain is full timepass. Umpire bhi ekdum confused hai."
The others laughed and answered the same way. Darshan, who spoke only Marathi at home and textbook English at school, tried to join. "The umpire is... very tension-mein?"
A pause. Then Yash slapped his back. "Tension-mein! Perfect, bro."
By the time the rain slowed, Darshan was trading lines with them. When Yash asked how he felt about batting at number seven, Darshan said, "Ekdum mast. But also thoda dar lag raha. Not scared, just... butterflies-wala dar." Yash nodded. "Same, yaar. Every match."
The umpire called them back, and they ran out together.

qa.q: Where did the team crowd while it rained?
qa.a: They crowded under the pavilion's tin roof.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling before he tried to join in?
qa.a: Darshan felt shy and left out, keeping to the edge as the newest player who spoke Marathi at home and textbook English at school.

qa.q: What helped Darshan feel part of the team?
qa.a: He took a risk by trying the team's mixed way of talking, and Yash welcomed his attempt with a slap on the back instead of correcting him.

qa.q: How does Yash see Darshan's mixed words?

qa.a: Salma felt ashamed and humiliated after the boys mocked her accent all week, so she whispered "I don't know" even when she knew the answer.

qa.a: A supportive peer, Abhinav, made her laugh about accents and practised with her, which slowly rebuilt her confidence to speak.

A group near the window snorted, and one of them whispered, "One doubt, one doubt," in a mocking singsong. For days the phrase followed him in the corridor.

qa.a: She went back and spoke in Maithili, asked about the family and waited her turn, which undid the status signal and treated everyone equally.

qa.q: How did the farmer likely feel when Anjali was served first?
qa.a: The farmer probably felt overlooked and small, pushed back in the queue because Anjali's English signalled status.

grounding: A young adult uses polished English with a local shopkeeper to signal status, then becomes aware of it and switches back.

"It says we love them and respect them," Mum said.

"Mehak, you asked how I got so patient with old people. Sit, let me tell you.
"When I was twenty, home from engineering college, my Ammachi would tell the same story every evening: how she came to Kottayam by boat as a bride, with one tin trunk. I knew it by heart. I used to finish her sentences to hurry her along.
"One evening I saw her face fall when I did it. She stopped mid-story and went to bed early.
"Next day, I tried something. When she started, I asked, 'Ammachi, what was in the trunk?' Her eyes lit up. Two saris, a Bible, and a jar of pickle from her mother. She'd never told anyone about the pickle.
"After that, I asked one new question each time. She didn't want to teach me anything, Mehak. She wanted to be listened to.
"When she died, Jomon, the one who finished her sentences, knew the most stories of all.

qa.q: What was in Ammachi's tin trunk?
qa.a: Two saris, a Bible, and a jar of pickle from her mother.

qa.q: What did Ammachi feel when young Jomon finished her sentences?
qa.a: Ammachi felt hurt and dismissed, her face falling so much that she stopped mid-story and went to bed early.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jomon's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Young Jomon asked what was in the trunk instead of hurrying her, and the new question made Ammachi feel heard and share a detail she had never told.

qa.q: How did the change affect Ammachi?
qa.a: Ammachi felt listened to and happy, her eyes lighting up as she shared new details.

grounding: An elder recalls learning, at twenty, to let a grandmother retell a story and ask a new question each time.

The power had been out for an hour in the Jaipur lane, and Kavitha sat with Lalit Uncle, her eighty-year-old neighbour, on his verandah with a candle and a hand fan. Her own phone was at five percent; her exam notes were waiting.
"Did I tell you about my tailoring shop near Johari Bazaar?" he asked.
He had, many times. The wedding sherwani, the rush before Diwali, the customer who never paid.
Kavitha glanced at her phone, then put it face down. "Tell me again. But this time, who was your first customer?"
Lalit Uncle blinked. "My first? A schoolteacher, Sharma ji. He wanted a kurta with pockets big enough for chalk." He laughed and laughed.
For forty minutes he talked. When the lights came back, he said, "You're a good listener, beti. My own sons only ask about my medicines."
Kavitha studied late that night, and didn't mind.

qa.q: How long had the power been out?
qa.a: The power had been out for an hour.

qa.q: What was Lalit Uncle feeling when he talked about Sharma ji?
qa.a: Lalit Uncle felt delighted and happy, laughing and laughing as he remembered his first customer.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She put her phone face down and asked a new question about the first customer, which made the old story fresh and made him feel heard.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had excused herself to study?
qa.a: Lalit Uncle would likely feel lonely and unheard, since he says even his sons only ask about his medicines.

grounding: A young adult lets an elder retell an old story and asks a new question, since the elder wants to be heard more than to instruct.

"Disha, you're always in a hurry when you show me the phone. Let your Nani tell you about Tejas.
"Last winter your cousin Tejas came to stay for a week. On the first day I asked him how to send a photo to your Mama in Canada. I expected him to grab the phone, press-press-press, and hand it back like you all do.
"He didn't. He sat beside me and said, 'Nani, you do it. I'll just tell you.' Slowly. Tap the little picture. Choose the photo. Tap the arrow. When I pressed the wrong thing, he didn't laugh. He said, 'Happens to me also.'
"I sent the photo myself. Your Mama called in ten minutes. I felt like a young girl again.
"Tejas even wrote the steps in big letters on a card and stuck it on my almirah. It is still there. Go and see.

qa.a: Tejas stuck it on Nani's almirah.

qa.q: What did Nani feel after sending the photo herself?
qa.a: Nani felt proud and happy, like a young girl again, especially when Mama called within ten minutes.

qa.q: Which of Tejas's choices made the difference, and why?
qa.a: He let Nani do the steps herself, explained slowly and didn't laugh at mistakes, so she learned and kept her dignity.

qa.q: How might Disha feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Disha might feel a little embarrassed about rushing Nani, and inspired to slow down next time.

The clinic in Pune was closing in twenty minutes, and the pharmacy counter had a queue. Chinmay had brought his uncle, Vaibhav Kaka, for a check-up. The doctor had spoken fast, handed over a printed chart of which tablets to take when, and moved on to the next patient.
In the noisy corridor, Kaka stared at the chart. "I can't follow all this. Just keep it with you."
Chinmay wanted to say, "I'll set reminders on your phone, done." Instead, he sat on the bench. "Kaka, let's do it together. You hold the chart. Which tablet does the doctor want in the morning?"
Kaka read it, slowly. Chinmay waited.
"Now open the clock app, the orange one. Tap the plus." Kaka's thumb hovered, pressed the wrong thing. "No problem. Back arrow."
They made it before the pharmacy closed. On the auto ride home, Kaka showed him the reminders. "I set these myself," he said.

qa.q: How long before the clinic closed?
qa.a: The clinic was closing in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Kaka have been feeling when he said "Just keep it with you"?
qa.a: Kaka likely felt overwhelmed and a little embarrassed by the fast advice and the busy chart, ready to give up and hand it over.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do that protected Kaka's dignity?
qa.a: He sat down, let Kaka hold the chart and press the buttons, and treated mistakes calmly instead of taking over.

qa.q: How does Kaka feel on the auto ride home?
qa.a: Kaka feels proud and capable, showing Chinmay the reminders and saying he set them himself.

grounding: A young adult explains a doctor's chart and phone reminders slowly under time pressure, letting the elder do the steps.

Shalini lived on the floor above Deepika Aunty in their Chennai apartment block. One evening Aunty knocked with her phone. "Your uncle's cousin sent a voice message, and I can't find where to hear it. My son says it's easy, but he's in Singapore."
Shalini felt the urge to take the phone. Instead she sat on the sofa beside her. "Aunty, you press. See the little triangle next to the message?"
"This one?"
"Yes. Now touch it."
The cousin's voice filled the room. Aunty laughed, then tried to reply. She held the microphone, then let go too soon. "Oh, it stopped!"
"It happens to everyone. Hold it the whole time you speak."
The second try worked. Aunty sat back, pleased. "Don't tell my son it took two tries."
"Two tries is normal," Shalini said. "It took me three the first time."

qa.q: Where does Deepika Aunty's son live?
qa.a: He is in Singapore.

qa.q: What does Aunty's request "Don't tell my son it took two tries" suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud of managing it herself but also a bit self-conscious about needing help.

qa.q: What small choice made Shalini's help respectful?
qa.a: She sat beside Aunty and let her press the buttons, and treated the mistake as normal instead of taking the phone.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had simply done it herself?
qa.a: The message would be heard faster, but Aunty might feel helpless and still not know how to reply next time.

grounding: A young adult explains a phone feature slowly without teasing and lets an elder do the steps, preserving her dignity.

Workshop supervisor's note, Saturday
Today I watched Yash, our twenty-five-year-old technician, try again to talk to Irfan sahib, who founded this workshop thirty years ago. Yash has been working on an idea to track spare parts on a simple spreadsheet. Every time he starts, Irfan sahib waves a hand: "You don't know the world yet, beta."
Today Yash did not argue or sulk, as he has before. He stood calmly and said, "Irfan sahib, I respect what you've built. I'm asking for ten minutes where you just hear me, and then you decide."
Irfan sahib looked surprised. He sat down. Yash showed him the sheet on his phone. Irfan sahib asked two questions, then said, "Try it for one month."
Afterwards Yash told me he'd been hurt for months, but this felt different.
What I will do next: I'll ask Irfan sahib to let Yash present the results at the monthly meeting.

qa.q: What idea had Yash been working on?
qa.a: Yash had an idea to track spare parts on a simple spreadsheet.

qa.q: How had Yash been feeling for months before this conversation?
qa.a: Yash had been hurt and unheard, since Irfan sahib dismissed him every time he started to speak.

qa.q: Which of Yash's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Yash calmly asked for ten minutes of real listening while showing respect, so Irfan sahib felt honoured rather than challenged and agreed to hear him.

qa.q: How might Irfan sahib have seen Yash's request?
qa.a: Irfan sahib was surprised, and probably felt respected enough by the calm request to listen instead of waving him away.

grounding: An adult's note shows a young adult repeatedly told he doesn't know the world, who calmly asks for a real hearing and shifts the pattern.

Sunday night
Nazia Khala came for lunch today and, as always, the moment I mentioned the PhD programme in Germany, she said it: "Zeenat, you don't know the world yet. Girls go abroad and come back strangers."
For two years I've either gone silent or snapped at her. Both end with me crying in the bathroom and her complaining to Ammi.
Today I did something else. I made her tea the way she likes, with extra elaichi, and sat beside her. "Khala, I love you. I know you worry. Can you give me fifteen minutes where you just listen to my plan? Then you can say anything."
She looked at me for a long time, then said, "Fifteen minutes."
I told her about the scholarship, the hostel, the Indian students' group, the calls every Sunday.
She didn't say yes. But she said, "Send me the hostel photos." That's new.

qa.q: What did Zeenat make for Nazia Khala?
qa.a: Zeenat made her tea the way she likes, with extra elaichi.

qa.q: How had Zeenat felt after earlier conversations with Khala?
qa.a: Zeenat had felt hurt and unheard, either going silent or snapping and then crying in the bathroom.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do differently, and why might it have worked?
qa.a: Zeenat calmly showed love, then asked for fifteen minutes of real listening, which made Khala feel respected rather than attacked.

qa.q: How might Nazia Khala feel about Zeenat's plan?
qa.a: Nazia Khala is still worried and protective, but she feels a little reassured, which is why she asks for the hostel photos.

I was staying with my brother-in-law Naveen and his baby, Mishti, the week my sister was away. Every morning I watched him bend close to her cot. He spoke slowly, eyebrows up, smiling with his whole face: "Good mor-ning, Mishti. Did you sleep?"
Mishti kicked her legs and cooed. "Aaah-oo!"
When he pretended to be sad, lips pushed out, she went still and stared.
Then he smiled again. She squealed.
Karthik, I told myself, the words don't matter to her. His face does.

qa.q: What did Naveen say to Mishti every morning?
qa.a: He said, "Good mor-ning, Mishti. Did you sleep?"

qa.q: What does Mishti going still suggest when Naveen pretended to be sad?
qa.a: It suggests she noticed the change in his face and felt unsure or puzzled for a moment.

qa.q: What could other caregivers take from Naveen's way of talking?
qa.a: Speak slowly with a warm voice and a face that matches the words, since babies read tone and expression first.

qa.q: What is it like for Mishti when Naveen talks to her this way?
qa.a: Mishti feels happy and engaged, kicking, cooing and squealing when he smiles.
